title.rendered: “Novelization Talk: Director Shingo Yamashita × Novelist Naruto Kiriyama”

content.rendered:
※This interview contains spoilers for the novelization.

With its Netflix release streaming to strong acclaim—and with sold-out screenings continuing after its theatrical debut—Cosmic Princess Kaguya! has been making waves across the industry.
Behind its production lay a creative “KASSEN,” where creators challenged and resonated with one another—much like the Libers of Tsukuyomi.

This time, we dig into behind-the-scenes stories from the novelization, which goes even further into the story’s hidden layers through Iroha’s perspective. We bring you a special conversation between director Shingo Yamashita and novelist Naruto Kiriyama.

“I can’t believe I’ve taken on such a difficult job”—What it means to write Iroha’s story

—This was your first time working together with Naruto Kiriyama on a project. When the project was initiated, what led you to choose him to write the novelization?

Yamashita: While this project does have some light-novel-like elements and aspects aimed at otaku audiences, I still wanted it to feel more like a “regular” novel—something with orthodox expression and a more natural authorial distance. After reading Naruto’s work, I felt his style looked at people and stories in a very neutral, even-handed way. That was probably the deciding factor.

—Naruto, how did you feel when you found out you’d be writing the novelization?

Kiriyama: Hearing that you saw my work that way makes me really happy—thank you. When I first received the setting materials and the footage, and then finished going through everything, my honest thought was, “I can’t believe I’ve taken on such a difficult job.” Not just the story, but the art, the action, the songs—and the setting and characters, too—everything already felt so complete. My first impression was honestly a bit of fear about what on earth I could add in novel form.

—Was it decided from the start that the novelization would be written from Iroha’s perspective?

Yamashita: We considered a lot of different options—there was even an idea to write it from Yachiyo’s perspective. But in the end, while keeping the story based on the anime, we aligned on a direction that focuses on emotions and digs deeper into Iroha’s family and past. The anime itself couldn’t fully convey those aspects, so we felt that if the novelization could communicate them properly, it would become something audiences could enjoy from another angle. I think we had a shared understanding along those lines.

Kiriyama: Right. The editor in charge also told me to emphasize the emotional side. I write in first person, so I paid very close attention to how Iroha thinks and how her emotions move. Even in the first meeting, I asked a ton of questions like, “Is this what Iroha is feeling in this moment?” What stuck with me was just how much you answered (laughs). Seriously—if I asked one thing, I’d get 20 or 30 things back. You’d answer anything, so I ended up asking far more than what I’d written down in my notes. Sorry for keeping you so long that day (laughs).

Yamashita: No, I was genuinely happy. It felt like you were asking exactly what I wanted someone to ask. I still remember that I thought, “Yes! That’s what I wanted to explain!” I could also really feel your passion and engagement, and I was so glad we’d asked you. And I think we just wanted to talk, too (laughs). We don’t get many chances to talk about the setting without restrictions.

—By the way, in your cover comment you wrote that you’d always wanted to write a story with a female protagonist. Why was that?

Kiriyama: My wife got me into shoujo manga, and I’ve come to like it quite a bit. I used to read only shonen manga, but shoujo manga portrays emotions with such fine detail that it shocked me—like it wasn’t even the same medium. I’d been wanting to try doing that in a novel for a long time, so getting this opportunity made me truly happy.

Yamashita: I see. That explains something (laughs). I think Cosmic Princess Kaguya! contains quite a lot of shoujo-manga-like sensibilities, so that’s probably where we resonated. Actually, a lot of the staff on this project are women—the original creator and the scenario writer are both women. In contrast, Naruto and I were among the few men working on this. As I supervised the novelization, I felt a kind of affinity with Naruto in the way he admires a feminine sensibility while still trying to stay close to it.

 

“Becoming Iroha”—Writing a novelization that stays close to the film

—Since this kind of work starts with an existing script and footage, I imagine turning it into a novel was different from writing your own original work. What approach did you take?

Kiriyama: Well… First of all, I knew I absolutely had to watch the footage. To write even a single letter, I’d play the video on a tablet, look at the script and the advice I’d received on my PC, do research on my smartphone, and then write on my main computer—basically a four-device setup. Since I wasn’t the only one involved in creating it, I felt what mattered was how closely I could stay aligned with the anime. It felt close to how I used to approach a role in theater—like “becoming Iroha.” That, too, brought me back to my theater days. Above all, it was just fun.

—As you supervised the novelization and experienced the work again in that form, what scenes left an impression on you?

Yamashita: First, the episode where Iroha, after being devastated by Kaguya returning to the moon, starts to pick herself back up—and when she finally comes back to school, she, Roka, and Mami hug each other in the hallway and cry. It was such a great addition. The producer still says they end up crying from emotion every time they read that part (laughs).

Kiriyama: I’d heard from you that when Iroha had been shut in, Roka and Mami were so worried they actually went to the front of her apartment. When I heard that, I decided, “I absolutely have to write this part.”

Yamashita: I think there are situations where you become so worried you start thinking, “What if they’re dead?” The relationship between Iroha, Roka, and Mami—and even the line, “We’re just glad you’re alive”—comes from experiences I’ve had, and people around me have had. It really felt like this is what would happen.

Kiriyama: Honestly, I thought it was impressive that the anime managed to hold back and not depict that scene on purpose.

—Related to that scene, the novelization also dug deeper into Iroha’s part-time job. Was that something that existed in the original setting?

Yamashita: The detail of the part-time job was something you suggested, wasn’t it?

Kiriyama: I really, really wanted to include the scene where Roka and Mami had come all the way to the front of Iroha’s place. But since it’s told from Iroha’s perspective, I needed a way for her to realize it. That led me to think I had to pull the thread in from her part-time job, and that’s how I landed on that setup.

Yamashita: I see—that was the logic. In the anime, there are very few scenes where Iroha talks with people other than Kaguya—like Roka and Mami. To portray Iroha’s personality, I do think scenes like that would have been better. But if we were going to include them, they would have had to be in the first half. However, even after cutting a lot, the runtime was still long. Anime is really hard (laughs).

—Is there anything else where you felt that they really complemented this well?

Yamashita: The sequence near the end—seeing Yachiyo’s 8,000 years of memories, and then the conversation between Iroha and Yachiyo through to the ending—was really great. It follows a slightly different flow than the anime, but it brought out the strengths of the novel form so well. I remember thinking it was a great novelization. I’ve wanted to tell you directly for a long time that I really, really love that whole progression.

Kiriyama: I felt like my pen really moved on those parts, but once I turned it in, all I could think was, “Was it okay…?” So hearing that makes me happy. You gave me so much information, and it made it easy to expand. The worldbuilding was incredibly thorough—like an intricate canal system—so it naturally became clear that if you let water flow here, then this was what would inevitably happen.

—In the novelization, the story ends slightly before the anime’s ending—just a little before happily ever after. Was that intentional?

Yamashita: This is something I want to ask Naruto, actually. I thought it was really good, but I was curious why you chose that.

Kiriyama: First, because it’s a novelization, I wanted to leave the ending to the anime. And also, I didn’t love the idea of ending in exactly the same way. So I stopped it there. Even the extra part, I felt, should be left to the anime.

Yamashita: That makes sense. I think Cosmic Princess Kaguya! is the kind of work that can end at many different points—you could probably continue it further, or you could end cleanly and sharply like the novelization does. It was fun to see a way of cutting the story that’s different from my own viewpoint, and it felt genuinely new to me. I also really love the final exchange between Iroha and Kaguya.

Kiriyama: Since it’s Cosmic Princess Kaguya!, I didn’t want it to end on a somber, quiet note. It had to be happy—so I ended it with a laugh.

—After working together as a team, what impressions did you have of each other as creators?

Kiriyama: The passion is just incredible. The energy I felt from him was on another level—that’s the biggest impression. It made me think that this was what top creators were like, and I felt an intense push to learn from it.

Yamashita: That’s praise I don’t get very often (laughs). I do believe you need passion at the core, so I’m happy to hear you say that. As for my impression of Naruto—you’re a professional, through and through. For a novelist, I imagine having the director’s opinions come in so strongly could feel constraining, but you accepted it very graciously. And you didn’t just accept it—you also brought out your own creativity, like in the scene with Roka and Mami. That sense of balance felt truly professional to me. All the way to the end—and even up to now—I feel we were able to work as one team. It felt dazzling, and I respect you deeply.

 

Digging into the Sakayori family—and an endearing cast

—You also posted that the novelization includes episodes about the Sakayori family. Could you tell us a bit more about what wasn’t depicted in the anime?

Yamashita: I’d given Naruto setting materials about the Sakayori family’s background at the beginning of the project. Even so, the personality of Iroha’s mother, Momiji, is extremely difficult to understand—she’s unusual, I think. There’s a scene in the novelization where she talks with Iroha on the phone, but in the anime that moment appears without any dialogue, so you can’t tell what they’re saying. As I supervised the novelization, I kept thinking how difficult it must be to put that into words. I think Naruto and I talked a lot about her. And just now I’m again thinking that this is probably the most challenging, most opaque part of the whole work.

Kiriyama: What left the biggest impression on me from our meetings was what you said about that phone scene: that it would never, ever be a happy moment where Iroha and Momiji reconcile. Personally, when I see a parent and child who don’t get along, I tend to assume they’ll reconcile by the end. But you told me, “I absolutely don’t want you to do that.” I remember how shocked I was—there was a real complexity there.

Yamashita: I think there are cases where, if something doesn’t get resolved, people feel like a plot thread hasn’t been paid off. But if they reconciled, it would change the character completely, so it’s something we simply can’t do—that’s what I meant to convey.

Kiriyama: I agree—understanding Momiji was the hardest part. To put it bluntly, she’s… a pretty terrifying mother (laughs).

Yamashita: Yeah, she’s terrifying (laughs).

Kiriyama: I’d also heard that if you put that into the anime as-is, the story would start in a much darker place—so you didn’t. It was difficult deciding how much to bring out in the novelization, and since I couldn’t exactly have Momiji herself appear directly, I think we ended up going in the direction of having her speak inside Iroha’s mind.

Yamashita: In the novelization, you referred to them as a kind of “Mom Quotes,” and they come up often—that was really good. Just reading them, you think, “What is wrong with this person?” and it almost looks like a gag, right? But the fact that it can look like a gag is exactly what makes it so serious for the person experiencing it. The balance is excellent—and it feels real.

—Are there any characters you wanted to dig deeper into?

Kiriyama: It’s not so much that I wanted to, but I think I could’ve written more about Iroha’s memory with her father, and also about Mikado. Oh—and I like Chuken Otako, too, so if she’d had more opportunities to appear, I think I could’ve written more about her as well.

Yamashita: Chuken Otako really is popular. Taro Yoneda also likes her. Amazing (laughs). I think there’s a lot to explore with Chuken Otako, too. If there’s another opportunity, I’d love to ask you again. Also—when we first talked, you said you liked Mami, didn’t you?

Kiriyama: Yes. I like her.

Yamashita: You were the first person who told me they liked Mami, and I remember how happy that made me. In a world full of people with these huge, overwhelming emotions, Mami is the one with the most ordinary sensibility. She’s a good person, and she’s set up as the kind of character who can have a clean, comfortable distance with others. So even ten years later, when everyone has their own ups and downs, Mami is the one who’s married, with two kids. So I think you saw from the start that she is someone who was raised with a lot of love.

Kiriyama: She is a very decent person, yes. And you told me she already had a boyfriend back in high school. When I heard that in our first meeting, my heart sank (laughs).

Yamashita: I’m sorry (laughs).

 

A “last resort” becomes the best scene—How Cosmic Princess Kaguya! completes itself across media

—What was the hardest part to portray in novel form?

Kiriyama: I remember struggling with the fireworks scene—capturing that atmosphere was hard. It’s such a great scene, so I watched the anime over and over, watched fireworks footage, too—turning that into words took a lot of time. That scene includes so much: Iroha telling Kaguya about her mother, Kaguya talking about returning to the moon. The anime pulls all of that together so neatly and coherently that the more I watched it, the more I kept thinking how insanely impressive what it’s doing is (laughs). If I’ve managed to do even some of that, I’d be relieved.

Yamashita: And it also includes Iroha’s father, too. I was happy you added those small supplementary details. One more thing I remembered: right before the last live begins, there’s the part where Iroha says, “If I were Yachiyo, would Kaguya have said she didn’t want to return to the moon?” That forms a kind of counterpart to the anime, and I felt that this is exactly the conversation they’d have. I love that part. Why did you decide to do it in that way?

Kiriyama: Since I was writing from Iroha’s point of view, if I did it the way the anime does—as a scene with just Kaguya and Yachiyo—then Iroha wouldn’t be able to be present in that moment. But I also felt I couldn’t leave that scene undescribed, so that’s how it ended up, as a bit of a last resort (laughs).

Yamashita: I never would’ve thought of that at all, so it felt like getting hit over the head in a good way. I thought, “Right, there was this option.” It happens all the time that a last resort ends up becoming the best scene (laughs).

—Lastly, could you share a message for the fans?

iriyama: I really tried to treat the emotional side with care—writing them not just as characters, but as people—so more than anything, I want readers to pay close attention to their emotions. I also focused on readability, and I think especially people who’ve watched the anime will be able to read it smoothly. I’d recommend it even to those who usually don’t read novels.

Yamashita: I’ve heard from a lot of people that, in the anime, the way we depict some of the drama that needs to be there still isn’t quite enough—and I do accept that, to a certain extent. But I think if you read this novelization, you’ll be able to receive the drama we couldn’t fully depict, such as the Sakayori family. Rather than a supplemental reader, it’s closer to the main story—something like two sides of the same coin. So I hope you’ll enjoy it alongside the anime. And if you can watch and read across all formats—the manga adaptation, the music videos, and more—complement one with another, and then come back and watch the anime again… that would make me happiest.
